steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Responses" section of a Wikipedia article on the Anthem medical data breach, covering how Anthem, commentators, state and federal regulators, and the courts responded.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Anthem's immediate response
- Public concern and calls for reform
- State insurance commissioners' investigation
- Federal (HHS) investigation and settlement
- Class action litigation and settlement

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Anthem's immediate response
  - hired Mandiant (cybersecurity firm) to review security systems
  - advised affected people to monitor accounts, stay vigilant
- Public concern
  - fears about theft of medical information generally
  - Harvard Law School writer: could spark reform of security practices and government data safety regulation
- State insurance commissioners' investigation
  - attacker's identity withheld; likely ordered by a foreign government (name withheld)
  - Anthem took reasonable measures before; remediation plan effective once discovered
  - breach started February 18, 2014
  - lead: Indiana Department of Insurance (DOI), Anthem's principal regulator (HQ in Indiana)
  - Indiana DOI hired independent auditors -> security assessment
  - [quote: auditors' conclusion on deficiencies and post-breach controls]
- Federal investigation (HHS)
  - $16 million settlement, by far largest HHS data breach settlement
  - [quote: HHS Director on largest breach / largest HIPAA settlement]
  - Anthem must do risk assessment, fix deficiencies, HHS oversight
- Class actions
  - approx. 100 private class actions, consolidated in California federal court, Judge Koh (respected authority on data breach litigation)
  - contested briefing over leadership
  - co-lead counsel: Eve Cervantez (Altshuler Berzon), Andy Friedman (Cohen Milstein)
  - Plaintiffs' Steering Committee: Eric Gibbs (Gibbs Law Group), Michael Sobel (Lieff Cabraser)
  - 2017: settled for $115 million, largest data breach settlement at the time
  - attorneys asked $38 million in fees; Koh allowed only $31 million

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Anthem hired a cybersecurity firm called Mandiant to review their security systems, and it advised people whose data was stolen to monitor their accounts and stay vigilant.

The data theft raised general fears about medical information being stolen. A writer from Harvard Law School suggested that the breach might spark reform of security practices and of government regulation of data safety.

Several state insurance commissioners conducted an investigation, which blames the breach on an attacker whose identity was withheld and claims that the breach was likely ordered by a foreign government, whose name was also withheld. The investigation also concluded that Anthem had taken reasonable measures to protect its data before the breach, and that its remediation plan was effective at shutting the breach down once it was discovered. It also says that the breach started on February 18, 2014. The Indiana Department of Insurance (DOI) was the lead investigator, because Anthem is headquartered in Indiana and so the Indiana DOI is Anthem's principal regulator. The Indiana DOI hired independent auditors to do a security assessment at Anthem, and the auditors concluded: "While deficiencies within Anthem’s cybersecurity posture were noted by the Examination Team, these deficiencies were not, in our experience, uncommon to companies comparable to Anthem in size and scope. While the pre-breach deficiencies impacted Anthem’s ability to reduce the likelihood of and quickly detect the Data Breach, the controls implemented subsequent to the Data Breach should improve Anthem’s ability to detect future breaches and enable Anthem to respond more effectively to a future attack than was the case in this instance."

- Federal investigation (HHS)
  - $16 million settlement, by far largest HHS data breach settlement
  - [quote: HHS Director on largest breach / largest HIPAA settlement]
  - Anthem must do risk assessment, fix deficiencies, HHS oversight
- Class actions
  - approx. 100 private class actions, consolidated in California federal court before Judge Koh (respected authority on data breach litigation)
  - after contested briefing: co-lead counsel Eve Cervantez (Altshuler Berzon), Andy Friedman (Cohen Milstein); steering committee Eric Gibbs (Gibbs Law Group), Michael Sobel (Lieff Cabraser)
  - 2017: settled for $115 million, largest data breach settlement at the time
  - attorneys asked $38 million in fees; Koh allowed only $31 million

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Anthem hired a cybersecurity firm called Mandiant to review their security systems, and it advised people whose data was stolen to monitor their accounts and stay vigilant.

The data theft raised general fears about medical information being stolen. A writer from Harvard Law School suggested that the breach might spark reform of security practices and of government regulation of data safety.

Several state insurance commissioners conducted an investigation, which blames the breach on an attacker whose identity was withheld and claims that the breach was likely ordered by a foreign government, whose name was also withheld. The investigation also concluded that Anthem had taken reasonable measures to protect its data before the breach, and that its remediation plan was effective at shutting the breach down once it was discovered. It also says that the breach started on February 18, 2014. The Indiana Department of Insurance (DOI) was the lead investigator, because Anthem is headquartered in Indiana and so the Indiana DOI is Anthem's principal regulator. The Indiana DOI hired independent auditors to do a security assessment at Anthem, and the auditors concluded: "While deficiencies within Anthem’s cybersecurity posture were noted by the Examination Team, these deficiencies were not, in our experience, uncommon to companies comparable to Anthem in size and scope. While the pre-breach deficiencies impacted Anthem’s ability to reduce the likelihood of and quickly detect the Data Breach, the controls implemented subsequent to the Data Breach should improve Anthem’s ability to detect future breaches and enable Anthem to respond more effectively to a future attack than was the case in this instance."

Federal regulators also investigated the Anthem data breach. This resulted in a $16 million settlement between Anthem and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which was by far the largest HHS data breach settlement. An HHS Director who oversaw the investigation said, "The largest health data breach in U.S. history fully merits the largest HIPAA settlement in history. Unfortunately, Anthem failed to implement appropriate measures for detecting hackers who had gained access to their system to harvest passwords and steal people's private information." The HHS settlement also required Anthem to do a risk assessment and to correct any deficiencies it found in its cybersecurity, and HHS would oversee Anthem's progress.

About 100 private class action lawsuits were filed against Anthem over the breach, and they were consolidated in California federal court in front of Judge Koh, who is a respected authority in data breach litigation. There was contested briefing over who should lead the litigation, and after it Judge Koh appointed Eve Cervantez of Altshuler Berzon and Andy Friedman of Cohen Milstein as co-lead counsel, and she appointed Eric Gibbs of Gibbs Law Group and Michael Sobel of Lieff Cabraser to head a Plaintiffs' Steering Committee. In 2017 Anthem agreed to settle the litigation for $115 million, which was the largest data breach settlement ever at that time. The attorneys asked for $38 million in fees for their work on the case, but Judge Koh cut the fee request and found that only $31 million in fees were merited.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Anthem hired Mandiant, a cybersecurity firm, to review its security systems, and advised people whose data was stolen to monitor their accounts and remain vigilant.[1,2]

The theft of the data raised general fears about the theft of medical information.[3,4] A writer from Harvard Law School suggested that the data breach might spark reform of security practices and of government data safety regulation.[5]

An investigation conducted by several state insurance commissioners blames the breach on an attacker whose identity was withheld, and claims that the breach was likely ordered by a foreign government whose name was withheld.[6] It also concluded that Anthem had taken reasonable measures to protect its data before the breach and that its remediation plan was effective at shutting down the breach once it was discovered.[6] It also marks the starting date of the breach as February 18, 2014.[6] The lead investigator was the Indiana Department of Insurance (DOI), Anthem's principal regulator, since Anthem is headquartered in Indiana.[7] The Indiana DOI hired independent auditors to conduct a security assessment at Anthem, which concluded, "While deficiencies within Anthem’s cybersecurity posture were noted by the Examination Team, these deficiencies were not, in our experience, uncommon to companies comparable to Anthem in size and scope. While the pre-breach deficiencies impacted Anthem’s ability to reduce the likelihood of and quickly detect the Data Breach, the controls implemented subsequent to the Data Breach should improve Anthem’s ability to detect future breaches and enable Anthem to respond more effectively to a future attack than was the case in this instance."[7]

Federal regulators also conducted an investigation of the Anthem data breach, resulting in a $16 million settlement between Anthem and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), by far the largest HHS data breach settlement.[8] An HHS Director overseeing the investigation said, "The largest health data breach in U.S. history fully merits the largest HIPAA settlement in history. Unfortunately, Anthem failed to implement appropriate measures for detecting hackers who had gained access to their system to harvest passwords and steal people's private information."[8] The HHS settlement also required Anthem to perform a risk assessment and correct any identified deficiencies in its cybersecurity, with HHS overseeing Anthem's progress.[8]

Approximately 100 private class action lawsuits were filed against Anthem over the data breach and consolidated in California federal court, before Judge Koh, a respected authority in data breach litigation.[9] After contested briefing over who should lead the litigation, Judge Koh appointed Eve Cervantez of Altshuler Berzon and Andy Friedman of Cohen Milstein as co-lead counsel, and appointed Eric Gibbs of Gibbs Law Group and Michael Sobel of Lieff Cabraser to head a Plaintiffs' Steering Committee.[10] In 2017, Anthem agreed to settle the litigation for $115 million, the largest data breach settlement ever at the time.[11] The attorneys requested $38 million in fees for their work on the case, but Judge Koh cut the request, finding that only $31 million in fees were merited.[12]
